children.translated_text: "That one alone, without a second" —
this is the statement of the <s>Upaniṣad</s> regarding <s>Brahman</s>.
Does it not deny the real existence
of anything other than <s>Brahman</s>?
Here we ask: in the expression 'without a second' (<s>advitīya</s>),
what type of compound is intended?
Is it a <s>tatpuruṣa</s> (determinative compound), or
a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> (possessive compound)? Let it be stated.
In the former [<s>tatpuruṣa</s>], the latter term
is expressed as the principal [meaning].
The word-meaning there is that <s>Brahman</s>
[is] other than that, or similar [to it],
or it would be opposed to that.
In all three cases, the other [entity] is not negated.
Whether [the second is understood as] different or similar,
the second is certainly established.
In the case of opposition, by [the existence of] the second,
a third or a first
<s>Brahman</s> is obtained, since that
is opposed to the second.
Therefore, all collections of meanings beginning with the third,
together with the first,
having been touched by the second in that way,
stand in their own meanings, unnegated.
Objection: the negative particle (<s>nañ</s>) negates
everything other than <s>Brahman</s>,
since the word 'second' (<s>dvitīya</s>)
is merely an indicator (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>) for everything.
Not so; for from this [compound], the negation
of [only] the second is understood.
It [the compound] speaks of what is other than that, or opposed to it,
or similar to it — [only] these.

children.text: na evaṃ niṣedho na hy asmād

children.translated_text: If it is intended that '<s>Brahman</s> is that which has no second at all,'
then
the characterizations stated [elsewhere] such as 'truth' and the like
would become non-characterizing [i.e., meaningless].
In [the compound] <s>advitīya</s>, if the scope is merely
the non-existence of the meaning of 'second,'
then, since the negative meaning is self-contained,
there would be no syntactic connection with the word '<s>Brahman</s>.'
The absence of a second therein
is not a qualifier of <s>Brahman</s>;
or if it is a qualifier, then that <s>Brahman</s>
[would be] a third or a first.
Everything follows as before
when [the compound] is analyzed as <s>bahuvrīhi</s>.
Those [entities] that are first [in rank] to <s>Brahman</s>, and
those beginning with the third in the three worlds,
stand in their own state, unnegated,
because of the non-secondness with respect to <s>Brahman</s>.
Moreover, when the <s>bahuvrīhi</s>
compound is resorted to,
the meaning of the negative particle, which functions [within the compound],
has no syntactic connection with another word-meaning.
When there is a relation to another meaning,
the genitive construction 'of whom' (<s>yasya</s>) is appropriate.
The non-existence of a second entity
is not <s>Brahman</s> nor a qualifier [of <s>Brahman</s>].
For being nonexistent, it cannot be <s>Brahman</s>,
nor can it serve as a qualifier.
Therefore, the real existence of the manifest world (<s>prapañca</s>)
is not negated by the non-duality scripture.
It is established by the force of its own valid means of knowledge,
and is also endorsed by scripture.
Therefore, the meaning of the scripture '<s>Brahman</s> is without a second'
is stated thus:
there was not, is not, and will not be
[any entity] worthy of being counted as its second.
One who is equal to or superior to it —
such a second is [what is] being counted [as nonexistent],
since this entire world is a mere fraction
of the display of its splendor.
How could it attain the status
of being called a 'second'?
Just as the <s>Cola</s> king is the emperor,
without a second on earth today —
this statement aims at precluding
a king equal to him,
but does not negate his servants, sons,
wives, and the like.
Similarly, the multitudes of gods, demons, humans,
<s>Brahmā</s>, and millions of cosmic eggs,
for the Lord of all, who is untouched
by afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), actions (<s>karma</s>), fruitions (<s>vipāka</s>), and the like,
who is a treasury of six qualities beginning with knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>),
whose splendor is inconceivable —
they are like scattered drops
from the ocean of the glory of <s>Viṣṇu</s>'s divine manifestation (<s>vibhūti</s>).
Who indeed, counting the seven oceans
by bending fingers,
could count the waves,
foam, bubbles, and spray?
Just as there is only one sun
without a second in the sky —
by this statement, the rays
of the sun are not being negated.
Just as the principal, in the enumeration
of things to be counted, is never counted [among them],
since the enumeration and the thing to be enumerated
exist separately, like a different category,
'One quarter of him is all beings;
three quarters are the immortal in heaven' —
thus declaring, [the scripture] established the entire world
in the status of 'being thus' [i.e., as a part of <s>Brahman</s>].
'Such is his greatness;
yet he is greater than that.'
'Where one knows nothing else' —
that is the fullness, the innermost [reality].
'It manifestly creates fear for him' —
these and other supreme scriptures [declare this].
For whom this entire <s>brahmāṇḍa</s> (cosmic egg), the whole universe,
is like an atom compared to [Mount] <s>Meru</s> —
such and similar [scriptures] declare
the status of everything as being such [i.e., subordinate to <s>Brahman</s>].
The world, both stationary and moving,
is a mere verbal designation (<s>vācārambhaṇa</s>),
being the product of modification; the immutable
root cause alone is real.
The effect is non-different from the cause,
like a spark from fire —
[as shown] by the extensive illustrations
of clay, iron, seed, and the like.
Fire could not burn already-burnt grass;
water could not submerge [what is already submerged];
nor could wind move [what is already moving] —
even with their power, without their operation.
'By knowing one principal [cause],
everything would be known' —
through such Vedic statements
and through reliable traditions (<s>āgama</s>) rooted in them,
this manifest world, consisting of conscious and non-conscious [entities],
is the self-attainment of <s>Brahman</s>.
Thus it is established: the divine manifestation (<s>vibhūti</s>) of <s>Brahman</s>
is not negated.
If it [the world] were negated, then, due to the falsity
of everything, all transactions
of the world and of the <s>Vedas</s> would be destroyed;
and so too would the cognition of <s>Brahman</s> [itself].
[The Advaitin's view that] there is no contradiction
even in falsity, because of 'empirical reality' (<s>vyāvahārikasatya</s>),
of perception and the like — this doctrine
was refuted even earlier.
And therefore, the world, by the cognition of
<s>Brahman</s>'s non-duality born from the <s>Upaniṣads</s>,
is not negated, because of being the manifestation (<s>vibhūti</s>)
of <s>Brahman</s> — this is established.
Objection: If the manifest world is real,
how can there be the cognition 'it does not exist'?
Or if it is unreal, how can
the cognition 'it exists' arise regarding it?
Similarly, for one and the same thing, being both real and unreal
is impossible due to contradiction.
When one encounters the contradictory pair
of cognitions 'real' and 'unreal,'
due to the absence of certainty
regarding either of the two meanings,
the <s>Jainas</s> accepted that the manifest world
is both real and unreal.
Giving priority to the attainment of reality,
[and explaining] the arising of the cognition 'it does not exist' [otherwise],
the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> established that the manifest world
is always real.
When confronted with the contradictory pair
obtained through the cognitions 'real' and 'unreal,'
in order to resolve the contradiction,
through the division into a real aspect and an unreal aspect,
some have declared the manifest world to be
indescribable (<s>anirvācya</s>) as either real or unreal.
Others have maintained the position that reality and unreality
are separately [attributed] due to differences in place, time, and the like —
for a pot and the like, thinking thus,
they have stated this systematic arrangement.
Thus, when doubt has arisen
from the clash of [these various] doctrines,
the determination is made therein
according to the view of the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s>.
If one understood non-existence in the very nature of the pot
and [also] existence,
then there would indeed be simultaneous reality
and unreality in pots and the like.
'This exists here now;'
'it does not exist' — since cognitions of this kind
arise due to differences of place, time, and condition,
they are not [cognitions of] 'exists' and 'does not exist' [with respect to the same thing].
Therefore, the reality and unreality of pots and the like
is established through differences of place and the like;
since [the apparent contradiction] is removed,
the [Advaita] thesis has no possibility here.
Objection: the relation with place and the like
is possible only for what is real;
the reality of the unreal is not accepted
[merely] from its relation with place and time.
Since relation requires two [real] bases,
the reality of the real would always obtain.
That the unreal should become real through causal factors
— through origination — is exceedingly difficult to maintain.
Therefore, the manifest world, having beginning and end,
is placed within the category of the real.
'What does not exist at the beginning and at the end
does not likewise exist in the middle either.'
Therefore, let it be accepted that what is of ascertained reality
is always real.
What is always unreal is forever unreal,
like a sky-flower, because of being fit for production.
There is no distinction between [something] unreal [now]
and what was unreal before or absolutely unreal.
Taking up [the case of] <s>Śvetaketu</s>,

children.text: tat tvam ity api yac chrutam
children.translated_text: what is heard as 'That thou art' (<s>tat tvam asi</s>) —
in its sixth chapter,
how can a primary meaning be possible?

children.text: tat tvam ity api yac chrutam

children.translated_text: The one indicated by the word 'thou' (<s>tvam</s>) is afflicted by
wretchedness, grief, and suffering, and is a conscious being;
the one [indicated by] 'that' (<s>tat</s>) is omniscient, of true will,
a limitless ocean of bliss.
How can there be identity between the meanings of those two [words],
like light and darkness?
Whether the word 'thou' refers to the marginal aspect (<s>taṭastha</s>)
(or the meaning of 'that' — the differentiating [aspect]),
the co-referentiality of the two words 'that' and 'thou'
with respect to a [shared] attribute is far from established.
Whether in the qualifications of being ignorant vs. omniscient,
of being afflicted vs. blissful, and the like,
or in [being] a qualifier of the conscious substrate (<s>ciddhātu</s>),
or in [being] an indicator (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>),
there would be a difference between the meanings of 'thou' and 'that'
because of the transference of contradictory qualities.
The thesis that consciousness is a single entity,
through the elimination of one part of what is expressed,
like 'This is that [same] ox' — [applied to] the words 'that' and 'thou'
is inelegant.
Because of differences in place, time, and condition,
even in a single substrate,
the transference of a contradictory pair [of qualities]
makes 'This is that [same] ox' appropriate.
But for the self-luminous conscious substrate,
in the conjunction of a contradictory pair,
there is no differentiating factor whatsoever
in place, time, condition, and the like.
If the self-luminous conscious self
is purged of all pairs [of opposites],
then, due to the absence of the delusion of the harm of duality,
scripture would become objectless [i.e., purposeless].
By this [reasoning], the possession of true desires,
being the cause of the world, and the like,
are superimposed on the Supreme through the limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>) of <s>māyā</s>;
while grief, delusion, and the like
[are superimposed] on the <s>jīva</s> (individual self) conditioned by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) —
[the claim that] there is no destruction [of these] —
this view of the minor knowers of <s>Brahman</s>
was refuted even earlier.
Whether [the limiting adjuncts such as] <s>māyā</s>, <s>avidyā</s>, and the like
belong to the essence of consciousness or to the qualified [<s>Brahman</s>] —
in the former case, there would be complete confusion
due to the non-distinction between the Supreme and the <s>jīva</s>.
In the latter case too, likewise;
even if consciousness is qualified,
since the essence of consciousness is without difference,
[and] through the limiting adjuncts of <s>māyā</s>, <s>avidyā</s>, and the like
appears as if divided and is deluded,
and is also qualified — [this is your view].
Do not the marginal (<s>taṭastha</s>) attributes
affect the essential nature at all?
For surely, <s>Devadatta</s> is not unharmed
by the cutting off of the head of the stick-bearer.
The residual establishment of consciousness alone
through the elimination of the non-conscious aspect —
that this is the meaning of 'That thou art' and the like
is also ungraceful.

children.text: atas tat tvam asi ity āder

children.translated_text: In the absence of non-<s>Brahman</s>-hood and non-selfhood,
the inner consciousness remains.
The two words 'that' and 'thou' pertain to the
identity of the <s>jīva</s> and the Supreme.
That identity, in its primary sense,
rests on two [distinct] real entities.
The conceptual alternative of difference and non-difference
that you have raised —
since non-difference and difference belong to [what is, on your view,] unreal [entities],
and since bondage [itself] is real, it is purposeless.
Non-difference is the destroyer of difference
between the two real entities that are its substrates;
difference is the mutual non-identity
of entities — thus of these two [terms],
having accepted the essential nature itself
of both the alternatives of difference and non-difference,
[if you attempt] negation — then by that verbal negation,
you are defeated by self-contradiction.
The conceptualizing about the relation of being different and non-different,
and about being real and unreal,
is beyond the reach of direct experience —
it is merely a drying of the throat [i.e., futile verbalism].
The cognition of blue in [something] blue
is the same as the cognition of blue in a blue lotus.
'This is a blue lotus' —
thus it directly shines forth to us.
Just as, even in the case of a contact-relation (<s>saṃyoga</s>)
that is known and within the range of the senses,
there is the error of imposing conceptual alternatives
of difference, non-difference, and the like through false reasoning,
so too, in the case of the identity-relation (<s>tādātmya</s>)
that is rooted in scripture and direct perception,
the false-reasoning conceptual error
is warded off by the rod of scripture.
And the faultless, non-personal (<s>apauruṣeya</s>) scripture,
out of great earnestness,
has repeatedly declared the identity (<s>tādātmya</s>)
of <s>Brahman</s> and the <s>jīva</s> as 'That [thou art].'
The liberated self, situated within the lake of <s>Brahman</s>'s bliss,
flourishes in happiness.
But in the absence of a distinct fruit-enjoyer from the fruit,
liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) would not be a human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>).
For if only the conscious substrate remains,
whose liberation would the fruit be?
Moreover, which consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>)
transforms into the form of the manifest world?
Not the cognition of a pot, for that is seen
even when it [the pot-cognition] is absent.
For it cannot be said that when it [consciousness] has not arisen
or has perished, the entire world
does not exist,
since [such a claim] would be contradicted by perception.
Nor is it another consciousness [that perishes], for even upon its destruction,
others are perceived.
Objection: consciousness is one and undifferentiated;
there is no cognition of difference in it.
Pots and the like are differentiated,
but consciousness is not, because it illuminates.
If the cognition of a pot does not shine
at the time of the awareness of cloth —
not so; for the pot does not shine,
but that [consciousness] clearly shines forth.

children.text: na evaṃ, ghaṭo hi nā abhāti

children.translated_text: If [you say that] the consciousness excluded from the pot
does not shine forth,
then by the expression 'excluded from that' —
is it the same [consciousness] that is meant, or something else?
If the same, it does shine; if another,
you do not state its shining.

children.text: kiṃ sa aiva ukta ātha va ītarat

children.translated_text: Moreover, for this self-luminous [consciousness],
which is formless — [there can be] from itself
no delusion of apprehending plurality,
apart from the plurality of objects.
Neither a real entity, nor a property of an entity,
nor perceptible, nor worldly —
the difference among knowable objects like pots
is merely of the nature of delusion.
If so, then the arising of apprehension
of difference in cognition is derived from that [delusion];
whence, all the more,
[comes] its connection with ultimate reality?
Moreover, for what is self-luminous,
the establishment of prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) and the like —
could it be from itself or from another?
From itself, it is certainly not appropriate,
because of the contradiction of non-existence
being untenable when [the thing] itself exists;
and because, for what illuminates by its own cause,
it is impossible even in the absence of itself.
because it has no other range,
consciousness is not [established] from another [source] either.
Moreover, of the knowable, difference and the like
cannot possibly be a property of consciousness,
like form and the rest; therefore consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>)
is non-dual, self-luminous.
Therefore, whatever is prattled
about its being different and so forth, based on [its supposed] difference —
this is the play of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) —
so the knowers of <s>Brahman</s> know.
Alas! This teaching of <s>Brahman</s>
shines forth for those who have faith;
but we are the faithless ones —
we who seek reasoning.
As the object of each individual knower,
mutually distinct from one another,
cognitions shine directly,
like pleasure, pain, and the like.
Of difference — which is revealed by its relata —
such as contact, desire, and the like for us,
difference does not intrinsically not exist,
nor is it non-perceptible, by consensus.

children.text: na hi bhedaḥ svato na asti

children.translated_text: If consciousness is accepted
as all-pervading, eternal, and one alone,
then either everything would always be [known],
or nothing would ever [be known].
For then the determination based on
the proximity or remoteness of the knowable
cannot be coherent, since consciousness,
like space, would have a pervasive extent.
Nor [can the determination be] through difference of causes,
since an eternal [consciousness] has no [causes].
Nor through plurality of essential nature,
since its oneness has been accepted.
And consequently, a deaf and blind person etc.
would perceive sound and the like;
and the distinction of teacher and student etc.
would be groundless — an absurd consequence.
Objection: For us, nothing whatsoever
is different from consciousness;
therefore, 'everything would always be [known]'
— this objection is entirely misplaced.
Reply: Tell us, O Sir — does blue and the like
not shine forth?
Or does blue etc., when shining forth,
not differ from consciousness?
On the first [alternative], the pleasant course
of the world and the Vedas [would be disrupted],
since nothing whatsoever — words, meanings, etc. —
would be manifest.
On the second, the desired
non-duality of consciousness would be undermined.
For if this manifold world of various forms
is of the nature of consciousness,
and if consciousness too is of that nature,
then plurality would follow.

children.text: sa āpi saṃvit tad ātma īti

children.translated_text: Nor can [you say] that, being the play of <s>avidyā</s>,
the determination of difference and non-difference [need not be made];
for that [<s>avidyā</s>], when touched by the fire of reasoning,
turns into a lac ornament [i.e., melts away].
For consider: if this <s>avidyā</s>
is held to be of the nature of the absence of knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>),
then, being of an indefinable nature,
it cannot determine anything.
If <s>avidyā</s> is a real entity distinct [from knowledge],
then the determination of difference is well-established;
the question of whether it is an entity or another entity
does not apply to it;
and that it is a reality different from knowledge —
that is a well-spoken statement.
If, on the other hand, even its being a real entity
is imagined through your delusion,
alas! then, this being the case, <s>avidyā</s> itself
would be knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>) in the ultimate sense.
Moreover, consciousness (<s>saṃvid</s>) is pure and non-inert;
this <s>avidyā</s>, however, is not of that kind.
Then for what reason is this [<s>avidyā</s>]
not determined to be something altogether different?
Furthermore, this <s>avidyā</s> of yours,
which is of the form of absence [of knowledge] and the like —
is the knowledge that is its absence consciousness,
or the knowable, or the knower?
If it is the knowable or the knower,
there is no cessation of [<s>avidyā</s>] through those,
for ignorance does not cease
through anything other than knowledge.
If [you say] it is consciousness itself — but then,
its arising is impossible according to you.
Moreover, if this [<s>avidyā</s>] is opposed to that [consciousness],
there is no possibility of it anywhere,
since the entire universe is pervaded
by non-dual knowledge alone.
If the absence, or the contrary,
of consciousness is also admitted,
then abandon far away your thesis
of the non-duality of consciousness.
Moreover, whose is this [<s>avidyā</s>]? Of the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>).
But who is the <s>jīva</s>? He who possesses it. If so,
then this amounts to a failure to resolve [the issue],
for it would be mutual dependence.

children.text: ko jīvo yasya sa īti cet

children.translated_text: For <s>avidyā</s> cannot arise from the <s>jīva</s>,
nor can the <s>jīva</s> [exist] without it.
Nor is the parallel with the seed and sprout [applicable],
since the origination of the <s>jīva</s> is impossible [in your system].
And if [<s>avidyā</s> belongs] to <s>Brahman</s> — then how is that [<s>Brahman</s>] omniscient?
How does it wander in delusion? You [should answer].
The dependence on the cognition of the body as the self,
which is produced by <s>avidyā</s>, does not [apply] to you
for the omniscient nature of <s>Brahman</s>,
since its naturalness is heard [in scripture].
If omniscience is false
because it is pregnant with the appearance of difference,
why is [the non-dual teaching] not equally false
for the very same reason — like other words and the like?
Just as the practice of other words,
number, and the like, which differentiate the scriptures,
are pregnant with the appearance of difference
yet are true — why is [omniscience] not similar?
If ignorance is possible even in one who is
omniscient and eternally liberated,
like darkness in fire, then
it could never be removed by anything.
That the validity of statements declaring omniscience etc.
is merely conventional (<s>vyāvahārika</s>),
while the validity of non-duality statements
is ultimate (<s>tāttvika</s>) —
we do not see any determining factor [for this],
apart from your obstinate insistence.
Being the locus and the counter-positive [of <s>avidyā</s>],
which are mutually contradictory —
how can <s>Brahman</s>, which is of a single taste,
be comprehended as existent?
If <s>Brahman</s> is the locus as the inner [self],
and the counter-positive in [another] form —
this difference of form, which has been produced
by the grace of <s>avidyā</s> [— if you say so],
but that [<s>avidyā</s>] too depends on that [<s>Brahman</s>] —
so there is mutual dependence again.
If [you say] because <s>avidyā</s> is unreal
... (this is not its characterization) —
where has it been observed by you that an unreal thing
serves as the defect of a real thing?
(Because of presupposing one's own thesis,)
the defect of mutual dependence [arises].
[You cannot avoid it] whether [<s>avidyā</s>] is real or unreal —
therefore this is not an answer.
Moreover, if <s>avidyā</s> is not a real entity,
how can it be a subject of practical dealing?
Nor is it [desired to be like] the practical dealing with
non-existent things like sky-flowers and the like.
And if it is said that it is not unreal either,
then reality is certainly established.
If it is meant that the negation particle negates
reality completely,

children.text: na apy avastv iti co(ktau tu

children.translated_text: what is first negated as real
by the complete negation particle
is then reproduced by the component [negation] —
thus [it becomes] real again.
Therefore [you should] never
wish to say [that <s>avidyā</s>] is neither real nor unreal,
that no difference whatsoever shines —
do not [say so] ever!

children.text: na sad-vacyaṃ na ca apy asat)

children.translated_text: Moreover, this <s>avidyā</s> that is resorted to
as the mother producing the maintenance of the world —
is it one alone,
or not one? Tell us this.
And is the <s>saṃsārin</s> (transmigrating soul) who is its locus
likewise one, or not one?

children.text: na ekā vā tad idaṃ vada
tatha aiko na eka eva vā

children.translated_text: If it is one, then that single [<s>avidyā</s>],
having been dispelled by <s>Śuka</s>'s knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>
already long ago,
your effort toward liberation is pointless.

children.text: sā ced ekā, tatas sa aikā

children.translated_text: Perhaps you think: <s>Vāmadeva</s>, <s>Śuka</s>, and the like
do not really exist,
so, since <s>avidyā</s> was not dispelled by their knowledge,
there is no present [<s>avidyā</s>] to be objected against.

children.text: syān mataṃ na eva te santi

children.translated_text: For the difference of liberated, unliberated, etc.
is imagined by my <s>avidyā</s>;
being seen [like a dream], like the manifold variety
of objects seen in my own dream.
And as for the statement that those [sages]
attained liberation through knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> —
that too should be countered by the reasoning
of dream-liberation talk.
But [we ask:] when someone else, by such an inference,
establishes the world as imagined
by his own <s>avidyā</s>,
how is that answered by you?
Whatever reason you wish to state
for [the world] having your <s>avidyā</s> as its cause,
that very same reason
would apply to him as well — like the proof of the omniscient one.
Thus, in your doctrine, which is undermined
by mutually contradictory statements,
you appear to be babbling
something or other like 'there is a face.'
And just as [your] fear of their liberation
resembles the talk of dream-liberation,
so too [it applies] to you as well —
hence your effort toward <s>mokṣa</s> is pointless.
Just as their liberation, which did not [really] occur before,
is [now] called 'having occurred' through knowledge of the self —
so too, [liberation] that will occur hereafter
through knowledge of the self —
even though it does not [truly] exist,
let it be designated as 'falsely going to occur.'
And you have the examples
of things seen in dreams as illustrations for this.
Objection: This is not undesirable to me —
that liberation will not come about —
because, since the self is eternally liberated,
[liberation] is eternally established.
Reply: Then this would be like
riding a corpse-spirit (<s>vetāla</s>) for pacificatory rites —
whereby the effort of acquiring knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>
is all the more pointless.
Objection: Though [liberation] is eternally present,
it is as if non-existent because it is obstructed by <s>avidyā</s>;
its manifestation
is accepted as the fruit of knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>).
Just as gold etc. in one's own hand,
when forgotten, is searched for;
and just as that very [gold] in one's hand,
when recognized, brings peace;
so too, from the non-cognition of the eternally established
essential nature of the self,
the <s>saṃsārin</s> (transmigrating soul) [suffers]; and through knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>,
its true nature is manifested.
Reply: Alas! What is this manifestation
that is held to be the fruit of knowledge,
of the self-luminous consciousness-entity,
which abides in the status of its own essential nature?
Is that manifestation consciousness itself? Or is it [the knowledge]
'<s>Brahman</s> exists'? And of what kind?
If it is the self-consciousness of the essential nature,
then it is eternal — hence it is not the fruit of that [knowledge].

children.text: saṃvit kiṃ sa aiva kiṃ va āhaṃ

children.translated_text: If the manifestation accepted
is the cognition 'I am <s>Brahman</s>,'
then that, for you, is knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> [itself] —
how can it be its own fruit?

children.text: kiñ ca sā tat tvam asy ādi
children.translated_text: Moreover, in your view, that [cognition] is produced
by the <s>mahāvākya</s> (great sentence) 'That thou art' etc.;
being originated, it is non-eternal —
so there would be fear even for the liberated.

children.text: kiñ ca sā tat tvam asy ādi

children.translated_text: Furthermore, those who know practical affairs
call that an obstruction (<s>pratibandha</s>)
which prevents an effect from arising
even when the complete cause is present.
Here, what is it that, having begun to arise
from its own cause,
does not attain origination
because it is obstructed by <s>avidyā</s>?
Not liberation, because it is eternally established.
Not even the cognition 'I am <s>Brahman</s>.'
For the complete cause
of the cognition 'I am <s>Brahman</s>'
exists in the <s>saṃsārin</s> (transmigrating soul) —
so how is it obstructed?

children.text: na brahma asmi iti dhīr api
na hi brahma āham asmi iti

children.translated_text: Since, due to the absence of its cause,
it does not arise at present —
it is not because it is obstructed.
Therefore that statement is misplaced.
Moreover, the [claim of] one individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) —
this does not accord with the actual state of things.
<s>Avidyā</s>, the association with it,
<s>jīva</s>-hood and the like are unreal according to you.

children.text: kiñ ca eko jīva ity etad

children.translated_text: The apparent oneness
is contradicted by appearance [itself],
for to us, transmigrating beings appear
by the thousands.
And the practical dealings occasioned by that
[multiplicity], which are unrefuted,
are perceived until the end of <s>saṃsāra</s>,
unlike the experience of dreams.
Therefore, even the [claim of] logical oneness
is contradicted by reasoning.
Activities inferred from differences of behavior —
[indicate] states of mind that are mutually opposed.
Other embodied beings, each having its own self,
cannot be denied.
Just as the fire etc. that is to be inferred
differs from [other] inferences,
[yet] are perceived — in the same way, how
are you not distinct from other <s>jīvas</s>?
If another knower is not inferred
from specific behavior,
all practical dealings, both worldly
and Vedic, would be destroyed.
Nor [can the differentiation] of the knowable and the knower
[be explained] through the difference of limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhis</s>);
for the same consequence would apply even within one's own body,
due to the difference of head, hands, etc.
For just as in that [body], when sensation arises
in the head, hands, feet, etc.,
there is unitary recognition [of the experiencer],
so too, for you, it would apply everywhere.
Experiences of previous births,
having long passed beyond the sufferings of hell
and the calamities of birth,
do not fall within the scope of memory.
When pleasure, pain, etc. arise simultaneously
[in different beings],
if there is confusion of substrates there,
how [can there be] the delusion of unitary identity?
Nor can worldly affairs (<s>lokayātrā</s>)
be accounted for by many <s>jīvas</s>,
each having its own <s>avidyā</s>,
each imagining its own visible world.
For they, unaware of what transpires for others,
each seeing only their own dream —
how could they carry on
that [worldly life] which depends on a single [shared] connection etc.?
Moreover, self-luminosity,
all-pervasiveness, oneness, and eternality —
which are accepted by you —
would undermine the non-duality of your consciousness.
These are not consciousness itself — they are its properties;
for even when consciousness is established,
dispute about them is observed;
and because those of such nature are differentiated.
Nor are they established through delusion
so that they would not contradict non-duality;
for those attributes are established by <s>Vedānta</s>
statements that reveal the truth.
If, on the other hand, bliss, self-luminosity,
eternality, greatness, etc.
are held to be the very essential nature of <s>Brahman</s> —
even there, let this be examined:
Inasmuch as '<s>Brahman</s>' is designated —
is it that alone? Or are bliss etc. [properties]

children.text: atha vā tasya te, yad vā
children.translated_text: of it? Or rather,
are they themselves bearing the name '<s>Brahman</s>'?

children.text: atha vā tasya te, yad vā

children.translated_text: On the first [alternative], the respective denotation
of those words would be futile in the Vedas and the world;
and by the reasoning stated earlier, there would be difference;
[and <s>Brahman</s>] being the cause of the world's origination etc. [would be problematic].
For the disputes of debaters about those [attributes]
presuppose <s>Brahman</s> [as already accepted];
on the second [alternative], by those very [attributes],
there would be accompaniment of <s>Brahman</s> [i.e., <s>Brahman</s> would not be non-dual].
On the third, <s>Brahman</s> would be fragmented,
since each [attribute] alone is the totality [of <s>Brahman</s>];
or alternatively, the aggregate would be <s>Brahman</s>,
like a forest is [an aggregate] of trees.
Greatness and illumination
are distinct even as they subsist in the sun;
therefore, there is nowhere a meaning of a statement
that would be a counter-example to their division.
If, by the exclusion of inertness, suffering, and the like,
the words 'knowledge,' 'bliss,' etc.
are applied to one [entity] alone,
then the existent is not accompanied by another.
But do those exclusions not exist at all?
Or do they exist? Or neither?
If they exist, the existent would have a companion;
[if not,] inertness etc. would be its nature [which is the opposite alternative].
The claim of being beyond both existence and non-existence
has already been refuted earlier.
And if that were the case, even <s>Brahman</s>
would not be distinguished from pots and the like.
Moreover, when non-inert-ness and other such [properties] to be excluded
fail to convey contradictory meanings,
those [properties] are not at all excluded,
just as by words having the same referent.
But when, regarding the counterpositive that is perceived,
there is a cognition that is merely of another entity,
that itself is [called] absence — here too
your [position] has a companion, say the wise.

children.text: sa aiva abhāva iti iha api

children.translated_text: How is the distinction of the differences among elements and their derivatives
from both existence and non-existence
to be ascertained? Is it indeed
through perception and the like, or from scripture?
The <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) — perception and the rest —
discriminate their own respective objects
as they arise,
to the extent that each is self-witnessed.
Just as, when blue is present before one,
a cognition of blue is not a tale of something else — the cognition
has a single form; for by that [cognition]
there is no apprehension of whiteness in a crystal.
Just as the cognition of sweetness in milk
is not at all a cognition of the bitterness of neem,
and all established practices —
both worldly and Vedic — are determinate,
it is true that there is apprehension, but if [you say] that this
has no basis in reality — that is not so;
if that [apprehension] exists, its basis
should be postulated, since it is an effect.

children.text: mūlaṃ na asti iti cen na tat

children.translated_text: If [you say it is] postulated [from] sense organs, inferential marks, etc.,
[then it is] because [differentiation] conforms to their existence;
the impossibility of simultaneity and sequence, and so on,
[applies] to both exclusion and positive determination.
The delusion that difference is not
perceptible because unity is impossible —
that [delusion arises] from failure to grasp
the mutual absence that constitutes difference and discrimination.
The very essential nature of entities
is ascertained through perception;
it would be the basis for the usage of difference
in relation to the counterpositive.
Just as a cognition of mere 'that' alone
is not the basis for the usage 'does not exist';
or just as the difference between short and long
[co-exists] in a single [object of] six finger-breadths,
so, by virtue of its possessing well-established
multiple modes and forms,
the reality of the perceptible manifold world
cannot be denied.
<s>Āgama</s> (scripture), being dependent on [prior] action,
is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) regarding such matters;
even if [it were] authoritative, since its word-meanings are incapable
of syntactic connection [in this domain], it does not convey [this knowledge].
It is not non-existent, because of apprehension; and the claim

children.text: na sad ity api yan na tat
children.translated_text: that it is not real because of sublation — that too is untenable;
why is it not real simply by virtue of apprehension?
From what sublation is the world non-existent?
Therefore, this <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) [that you posit]
is itself dependent on <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) for you.

children.text: na sad ity api yan na tat

children.translated_text: Moreover, the property characterized as <s>mithyātva</s> (falsity)
of the manifold of differences —
is it false or ultimately real?
The first option does not [work] straightforwardly;
if that [mithyātva] is itself false,
the reality of the manifold is hard to deny;
and if it is ultimately real,
by that very [fact] your non-duality is destroyed.
All the <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) indeed
discriminate their own respective objects as stated,
from non-existent [objects] and from other objects,
and shine [as valid] for us.
For here, when the cognition arises
that 'this pot exists',
that [cognition] does not then admit
the non-existence of that [pot], nor [its being] cloth-ness.
Now, what was said [with] 'exists' — is that
mere 'that' [i.e., bare existence], or is 'pot' also
something different? If [it is] mere 'that',
then non-duality of [bare] existence follows;
if [it is] something different, then what is established
is [something] different from both existent and non-existent.

children.text: nanv asti iti yad uktaṃ kiṃ

children.translated_text: If so, then '<s>Brahman</s> exists' —
this Upaniṣadic teaching about <s>Brahman</s>
would, like [the case of] the pot, be indeterminable
as either existent or non-existent — which would be your consequence.
By Vedic descriptions such as bliss, truth, and knowledge,
the fact that <s>Brahman</s> too
is not otherwise [i.e., has positive attributes]
has been established by you yourself in this way.
The statement that the manifold is different from
both existent and non-existent is thereby undermined;
for whatever is said about anything in any way,
all of that would apply to everything equally.
Therefore, the cognition 'it exists',
arising with respect to pots and the like,
reveals the ultimate reality
of the constitution of each respective object.
The existence of objects established through their own
respective forms, grounded in
exclusion from homogeneous
and heterogeneous [classes] —
that is <s>sattā</s> (existence), not an independent other [entity];
how then can there be talk of non-duality there?
And the multiform
apprehension cannot be denied;
that the knowable is not a property of cognition —
this is what was stated earlier.
By that [argument] too, has something of
cognition been established by you, or not?
If it has, there would be partiality;
if not, your effort is fruitless.
Therefore, cognitions whose difference is clearly
manifest by their own nature,
do not become one with external [objects]
such as pots that abide as they are.
The <s>sahopalambhaniyama</s> (rule of co-apprehension)
is indeed not [established] by each individual cognition;
for if it were not so, everything along with [its] universal
would be the object of [every] cognition.
From the <s>sahopalambhaniyama</s> (rule of co-apprehension),
there is no object other than cognition —
that which is independent [of anything else],
<s>svaprakāśa</s> (self-luminous), that indeed
is what is denoted by the word '<s>svayamprakāśatā</s>' (self-luminosity),
so the learned declare.
That which, even when [cognition] does not shine,
the so-called object does not shine —
that [object] is not something other than that [cognition],
like a false moon [is not different] from the [real] moon.
And when cognition does not shine,
neither self nor object appears;
thus, that the manifold world is a transformation of cognition
it clearly proclaims.
Do not thus disparage inferential [reasoning]!
By perception, which is stronger,
those whose differences are upheld [by perception]
do not follow inference [that contradicts perception].
For 'I know this' —
as mutually distinct from one another, clearly
a triad shines directly;
this is self-witnessed by all.

children.text: tathā hi idam ahaṃ vedmi ity

children.translated_text: And inference does not operate
in opposition to perception;
for the non-hotness of fire
is not inferred from [its] being a substance.
Moreover, this reason [i.e., co-apprehension] is contradicted,
since the co-existence of the two [is admitted];
for even according to you, cognition does not
shine together with its own self.
A pure, transparent stream of consciousness alone,
free from the disturbance of blue and the like,
shines in deep sleep and such [states]; but an object
is not thus [manifest] separately from cognition —
therefore cognition is real,
while the cognized object is unreal — so [the Yogācāra says].
This is the babble of one who has not considered
the self-contradiction of his own words;
for the <s>sahopalambhaniyama</s> (rule of co-apprehension)
is thereby, given this [admission], undermined.
Since that without which something shines
also shines without that [other thing],
even without a pot, the pot itself shines
just as [it shines] without a cloth.
